A Difference-In-Differences Study of the Effects of a New Abandoned Building 
Remediation Strategy on Safety.

(2)Social and Behavioral Sciences, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, CT,

Erratum in
    PLoS One. 2015 Aug 20;10(8):e0136595. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0136595.

Vacant and abandoned buildings pose significant challenges to the health and 
safety of communities. In 2011 the City of Philadelphia began enforcing a Doors 
and Windows Ordinance that required property owners of abandoned buildings to 
install working doors and windows in all structural openings or face significant 
fines. We tested the effects of the new ordinance on the occurrence of crime 
surrounding abandoned buildings from January 2011 to April 2013 using a 
difference-in-differences approach. We used Poisson regression models to compare 
differences in pre- and post-treatment measures of crime for buildings that were 
remediated as a result of the ordinance (n = 676) or permitted for renovation (n 
= 241), and randomly-matched control buildings that were not remediated (n = 
676) or permitted for renovation (n = 964), while also controlling for 
sociodemographic and other confounders measured around each building. Building 
remediations were significantly associated with citywide reductions in overall 
crimes, total assaults, gun assaults and nuisance crimes (p < 0.001). Building 
remediations were also significantly associated with reductions in violent gun 
crimes in one city section (p < 0.01). At the same time, some significant 
increases were seen in narcotics sales and possession and property crimes around 
remediated buildings (p < 0.001). Building renovation permits were significantly 
associated with reductions in all crime classifications across multiple city 
sections (p < 0.001). We found no significant spatial displacement effects. 
Doors and windows remediation offers a relatively low-cost method of reducing 
certain crimes in and around abandoned buildings. Cities with an abundance of 
decaying and abandoned housing stock might consider some form of this structural 
change to their built environments as one strategy to enhance public safety.

Sustainability of violence prevention after a randomized vacant lot greening 
intervention in Philadelphia: A 10-y follow-up.

Asa N(1)(2), Zewdie HY(1)(3), Omidvar Tehrani S(4), Beverly M(5), Carroll-Scott 
A(5)(6), Rowhani-Rahbar A(1)(2), Rundle AG(7), Kondo MC(8), Clougherty JE(9),

(5)Drexel Urban Health Collaborative, Dornsife School of Public Health, Drexel

(6)Department of Community Health and Prevention, Dornsife School of Public

(7)Department of Epidemiology, Mailman School of Public Health, Columbia

(8)United States Department of Agriculture Forest Service, Philadelphia, PA

(9)Department of Environmental and Occupational Health, Dornsife School of 
Public Health, Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA 19104.
(10)Centers for Studies in Demography and Ecology, University of Washington, 
Seattle, WA 98195.

Vacant lot greening has been shown to reduce violence and crime in the 
short-term [C. C. Branas et al., Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 115, 2946-2951 
(2018)]. We assessed the 10-y impact of a 2013 clustered randomized controlled 
trial (RCT) of lot greening in Philadelphia on violence and crime. We measured 
lot greening by treatment assignment from the original 2013 cluster RCT and a 
longitudinal greening score to assess the sustainability of the treatment 
assignment from 2012 through 2023. Our outcomes were the annual reported total 
crime, violent crime, and firearm violent crime per square mile at each lot. We 
conducted intent-to-treat and contamination-adjusted intent-to-treat analyses to 
estimate the local average treatment effect on relative change in crime. Lots 
randomized to the full greening intervention remained greener over time compared 
to other lots. In intent-to-treat analyses, compared to lots that received no 
intervention, lots that received any intervention had a 9% decrease in density 
of any crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.96) and a 9% decrease in violent 
crime (estimate = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.86, 0.97) per square mile per year. In 
contamination-adjusted analyses, compared to lots without sustained greening 
treatment, lots with sustained greening treatment had a 12% decrease in density 
of any crime (estimate = 0.88, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.93) and an 11% decrease in 
density of violent crime (estimate = 0.89, 95%CI = 0.83, 0.95) per square mile 
per year. Even after a decade, vacant lot greening continues to prevent 
violence.

equity may be a promising target for public health interventions. The present 
study was a cluster randomized controlled trial to test the impact of 
remediating vacant and abandoned properties on factors related to health 
mindset-including well-being, health interconnectedness, social capital markers, 
neighborhood disorder, and worry-as well as direct and indirect violence 
experiences and the moderating role of racial and income segregation on 
outcomes. A residential cohort of 405 participants from 194 randomly assigned 
geographic clusters was surveyed over five waves from 2019 to 2023. Compared to

Mural Art and Youth Victimization of Firearm Violence: A Quasi-Experimental 
Analysis.

Bhatia S(1)(2), Lee DB(1)(3), Wyatt R(4)(5), Crimmins H(1), Tharp S(6), Byron 
MC(1), Howard BJ(7), Zimmerman MA(8)(9), Prophet J(10).

Author information:
(1)Institute for Firearm Injury Prevention, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 
USA.
(2)Center for Neighborhood Engaged Research and Science, Northwestern 
University, Evanston, USA.
(3)School of Social Work, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA.
(4)School of Public Health, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA.
(5)School of Information, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA.
(6)Stamps School of Art & Design, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA.
(7)Detroit City Walls, Detroit, USA.
(8)Institute for Firearm Injury Prevention, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 
USA. marcz@umich.edu.
(9)School of Public Health, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA. 
marcz@umich.edu.
(10)Sheffield Hallam University, Sheffield, UK.

Community violence and firearm violence are persistent public health challenges 
in the USA. Guided by Busy Streets Theory (BST), we examine the effects that 
public art in the form of murals on police incidents involving youth as victims. 
We studied 248 mural sites in Detroit, Michigan, and used a 3:1 propensity score 
matching to identify sites without a mural for comparison purposes. We used 
kernel density of police incident data at 100, 200, 300, and 400 m bandwidth 
distances from the centroid of blocks with at least one mural identified by our 
community partners. We used Google Street View to verify if any control sites 
had a mural or public art that we were not aware of and removed them from the 
study. We also included several covariates (e.g., zoning, prior year police 
incident data, neighborhood disadvantage variables) in our analysis to eliminate 
alternative explanations. Our results indicated fewer police incidents for youth 
violent crime victimization post mural installation across bandwidths with 
decreasing effects for further distances. Our findings support BST because 
public art is a physical display of neighborhood attention and local care for 
the neighborhood and expands research on greening and vacant lot remediation by 
demonstrating that aesthetic enhancement of neighborhoods by public art can have 
similar salutary effects on violent crime victimization.
